items.stem: Which of the following political ideas best reflects Coolidge's perspective in the passage?
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)

options.text: Progressive taxation is a fair way to redistribute wealth.
Government should remain limited in size and scope.
A larger, more active government best secures social justice.
Government properly decides how citizens may use their property.

items.explanation: Coolidge treats taxation as a threat to a basic right of ownership. That view fits limited government: low taxes and low spending. It is the opposite of using taxes to redistribute wealth or expand government.

items.stem: Which of the following later presidents would most likely have shared Coolidge's sentiments?
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)
items.explanation: Reagan, like Coolidge, argued for limited government and lower taxes, and he openly admired Coolidge. Roosevelt, Johnson, and Obama all expanded the federal government's role.

items.stem: The ideas expressed in the passage were most directly shaped by which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)

options.text: The broad economic prosperity of the 1920s
The rapid growth of the welfare state in the 1920s

items.explanation: Coolidge spoke in 1924, when the country was prospering, and he credited that prosperity to keeping government out of the way of business. There was no welfare state yet, and no mass hardship in the mid-1920s.

items.stem: In the passage, Coolidge is most directly reacting against which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)

options.text: The economic policies of his predecessor, Warren G. Harding
The strength of radical politics after the Russian Revolution
The Progressive Era expansion of government's role

items.explanation: Coolidge's attack on taxation targets the legacy of the Progressives, who had greatly expanded federal regulation and introduced the income tax. Harding largely shared Coolidge's outlook; the Populists were a 1890s movement.

items.stem: Which of the following most directly reflects de Bry's perspective in the image?
items.stimulus:
Questions 5–8 refer to the following image.

[An engraving by Theodor de Bry, 'The Natives of Florida Worship the Column Erected by the Commander on His First Voyage,' Grand Voyages, 1591: a stone column stands on a Florida shore while a crowd of Timucua Native Americans kneel before it in worship, as French soldiers and officers look on.]

options.text: The natives of Florida are primitive and superstitious.
The natives of Florida are deeply Christian.
Europeans are unjustly exploiting the natives.
Conflict between natives and Europeans is inevitable.

items.explanation: De Bry shows the Timucua worshipping a French monument, framing them as simple people awed by European symbols. The image flatters European power rather than criticizing it or predicting war.

items.stem: De Bry's engraving is best understood as an expression of which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 5–8 refer to the following image.

[An engraving by Theodor de Bry, 'The Natives of Florida Worship the Column Erected by the Commander on His First Voyage,' Grand Voyages, 1591: a stone column stands on a Florida shore while a crowd of Timucua Native Americans kneel before it in worship, as French soldiers and officers look on.]

options.text: European doubts about the value of exploration
European curiosity about the wider world

items.explanation: De Bry produced dozens of engravings of New World peoples for a European audience hungry for news of the Americas. The image feeds curiosity about distant lands and peoples, not fear of them or doubt about exploration.

items.stem: The column erected by the French commander in the image most directly signified which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 5–8 refer to the following image.

[An engraving by Theodor de Bry, 'The Natives of Florida Worship the Column Erected by the Commander on His First Voyage,' Grand Voyages, 1591: a stone column stands on a Florida shore while a crowd of Timucua Native Americans kneel before it in worship, as French soldiers and officers look on.]

options.text: European plans to convert the Native Americans to Christianity
European hopes for trade in new products
European claims to political control over new territory
European interest in sharing Native American culture

items.explanation: Ribault's column was a marker of possession: a public claim that France owned the land. European powers used such monuments to announce sovereignty, the legal basis for colonization.

items.stem: Rivalries among European powers soon led the French settlement in Florida to be destroyed by which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 5–8 refer to the following image.

[An engraving by Theodor de Bry, 'The Natives of Florida Worship the Column Erected by the Commander on His First Voyage,' Grand Voyages, 1591: a stone column stands on a Florida shore while a crowd of Timucua Native Americans kneel before it in worship, as French soldiers and officers look on.]
items.explanation: Spain, which claimed Florida, attacked the French Huguenot colony at Fort Caroline in 1565 and massacred its inhabitants. Neither the English nor the Dutch operated in Florida at that time.

items.stem: Which of the following would most likely have supported the perspective Riis expresses in the passage?
items.stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)
items.explanation: Riis exposes the misery of poor working women to demand reform, exactly the goal of Progressive reformers. Social Darwinists would have called such poverty natural, and business owners had little interest in publicizing it.

items.stem: The situation of the young women in the passage is most directly comparable to that of which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)

options.text: Enslaved people in the antebellum South

items.explanation: Both groups were low-paid workers fighting for better wages and conditions: the young women in Riis's account and the 1930s autoworkers who staged sit-down strikes. The other choices involve revolutions, slavery, or farmers, not industrial wage labor.

items.stem: Concerns like those Riis expresses most directly led to which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)
items.explanation: Muckraking exposes of women's working conditions fueled the Progressive drive for protective labor laws, such as limits on women's working hours. Immigration restriction and suffrage had different causes; antitrust targeted monopolies.

items.stem: Riis's investigative work on the lives of the poor is most directly associated with which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)
items.explanation: Riis was a classic muckraker: a journalist who exposed urban poverty and corruption to spur reform. Yellow journalism sensationalized for sales, abolitionism was an earlier movement, and Riis was not a socialist.

items.stem: The Zenger trial is best described as which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)

options.text: A colonial dispute over British taxation policy
An early attack on the institution of slavery
A landmark case concerning voting rights
A landmark case concerning freedom of expression

items.explanation: Zenger was tried for seditious libel after printing criticisms of New York's royal governor. Hamilton's acquittal victory established that truthful criticism of officials should not be punished, a milestone for press freedom.

items.stem: Hamilton's argument in the passage assumes which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)

options.text: Free men enjoy rights broader than those held in other countries.
People in other countries enjoy more rights than Americans.
Natural rights are merely ideas without real force.
Rights are grants bestowed by the government.

items.explanation: Hamilton appeals to the natural rights of free men and the liberties of British subjects, arguing the jury should defend them. He treats rights as inherent, not as gifts of government, and appeals to an American sense of liberty.

items.stem: The Zenger case is best compared to which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)

options.text: Lincoln's suspension of habeas corpus during the Civil War
The 1971 attempt to block the Pentagon Papers
The 1886 trial of the Haymarket Square bombers
The Supreme Court's Brown v. Board of Education decision

items.explanation: Both Zenger and the Pentagon Papers cases pitted the government's power to punish publication against the press's freedom to criticize officials. Habeas corpus, Haymarket, and Brown involve different rights and issues.

items.stem: Hamilton's acquittal of Zenger most directly reflected which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)

options.text: Colonial desires for independence from Great Britain
A long colonial tradition of self-rule
The weakening of economic ties between Britain and America

items.explanation: The jury's refusal to defer to the royal governor's judges showed colonists accustomed to governing themselves through assemblies and juries. Independence was still decades away, and the case was about speech, not trade.

items.stem: Which of the following best expresses Thomas Nast's perspective in the cartoon?
items.stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options.text: The Reconstruction of the South is succeeding.
The government is failing to protect freed Black people.
Reconstructing Southern society was a mistake.

items.explanation: Nast shows armed white-supremacist groups terrorizing a Black family, warning that freedpeople are being returned to something 'worse than slavery.' He is demanding stronger federal protection, not celebrating Reconstruction.

items.stem: The conditions Nast depicts contributed most directly to which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options.text: The Homestead Act offering settlers free land
The Supreme Court's Plessy v. Ferguson decision

items.explanation: The failure to stop white-supremacist violence left segregation to harden into law, culminating in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which upheld 'separate but equal.' The Fifteenth Amendment predates the cartoon; the Homestead Act is unrelated.

items.stem: The Southerners in the cartoon wanted a 'Union' in which sovereignty rested with which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options.text: The anti-nullification nationalism of Andrew Jackson.

items.explanation: Nast's 'Union as it was' is the states'-rights Union of the Lost Cause: each state supreme within its borders, free to subordinate Black citizens. That doctrine had justified slavery before the war and segregation after it.

items.stem: Nast's cartoon most directly reflects the continuity of which of the following debates in U.S. history?
items.stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options.text: Debates over the use of military power
Debates over the role of political parties

items.explanation: Nast was intervening in the struggle over Black Americans' rights, a debate running from slavery through Reconstruction to the modern civil rights era. The cartoon says nothing about the military, guns, or parties as institutions.

items.stem: Ferraro's nomination for vice president most directly continued which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following quotation.

In her vice-presidential nomination acceptance address of July 19, 1984, Geraldine Ferraro described herself as the daughter of working Americans and of a woman whose highest goal was a future for her children, telling the nation's oldest political party that the future was within reach. —Paraphrase of Geraldine Ferraro, acceptance address, July 19, 1984 (abridged)

options.text: The successful assimilation of immigrants into the United States
The struggle for civil rights for ethnic minorities
Expanded economic and political opportunities for women
The increasing democratization of the nomination process

items.explanation: As the first woman on a major-party national ticket, Ferraro embodied the women's movement's gains in political access. Her nomination was about gender, not immigration, ethnic minorities, or how nominees are chosen.

items.stem: The political ideas expressed in the passage most directly resemble those of which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following quotation.

In her vice-presidential nomination acceptance address of July 19, 1984, Geraldine Ferraro described herself as the daughter of working Americans and of a woman whose highest goal was a future for her children, telling the nation's oldest political party that the future was within reach. —Paraphrase of Geraldine Ferraro, acceptance address, July 19, 1984 (abridged)

options.text: Colonial opponents of British taxation in the 1760s and 1770s

items.explanation: Ferraro was a liberal Democrat whose program of active government helping working families descends from the New Deal tradition. Colonial tax protesters, abolitionists, and 1920s Republicans held very different views of government's role.

items.stem: Ferraro's message would most directly have strengthened which of the following during the 1980s?
items.stimulus:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following quotation.

In her vice-presidential nomination acceptance address of July 19, 1984, Geraldine Ferraro described herself as the daughter of working Americans and of a woman whose highest goal was a future for her children, telling the nation's oldest political party that the future was within reach. —Paraphrase of Geraldine Ferraro, acceptance address, July 19, 1984 (abridged)

options.text: Opposition to the Reagan administration's military buildup
Efforts to reform the welfare system
Support for the administration's Cold War policies

items.explanation: As a Democrat running against Reagan, Ferraro's liberal platform opposed his policies, including the massive defense buildup. Deregulation and Cold War hawkishness were Reagan's own positions, not hers.

items.stem: Geraldine Ferraro is most directly comparable to which of the following women?
items.stimulus:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following quotation.

In her vice-presidential nomination acceptance address of July 19, 1984, Geraldine Ferraro described herself as the daughter of working Americans and of a woman whose highest goal was a future for her children, telling the nation's oldest political party that the future was within reach. —Paraphrase of Geraldine Ferraro, acceptance address, July 19, 1984 (abridged)
items.explanation: O'Connor, the first woman on the Supreme Court (1981), and Ferraro both broke gender barriers in national public life in the early 1980s. Adams, Addams, and Parks belong to different eras and roles.

items.stem: The westward movement Parkman describes led most directly to which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 25–28 refer to the following quotation.

"MARY ELLIS DIED MAY 7th, 1845 … Such tokens were of common occurrence … we saw close before us the emigrant caravan, with its heavy white wagons creeping on in their slow procession, and a large drove of cattle following behind. … The women were divided between regrets for the homes they had left and apprehension of the deserts and savages before them." —Francis Parkman, The Oregon Trail: Sketches of Prairie and Rocky-Mountain Life, 1849 (abridged)

options.text: The Dred Scott Supreme Court decision

items.explanation: The overland migration Parkman witnessed embodied the popular demand for western land that Congress answered with the Homestead Act of 1862, granting 160 acres to settlers. The Northwest Ordinance (1787) and Indian Removal (1830) came earlier; Dred Scott was about slavery in the territories.

items.stem: The actions of the westward migrants in the passage most directly reflected the influence of which of the following political ideals?
items.stimulus:
Questions 25–28 refer to the following quotation.

"MARY ELLIS DIED MAY 7th, 1845 … Such tokens were of common occurrence … we saw close before us the emigrant caravan, with its heavy white wagons creeping on in their slow procession, and a large drove of cattle following behind. … The women were divided between regrets for the homes they had left and apprehension of the deserts and savages before them." —Francis Parkman, The Oregon Trail: Sketches of Prairie and Rocky-Mountain Life, 1849 (abridged)
items.explanation: The migrants' belief that the continent was theirs for the taking was Manifest Destiny, the 1840s creed that Americans were destined to spread across North America. Popular sovereignty concerned slavery in territories; Jacksonian Democracy was about political participation.

items.stem: The experiences of the people Parkman encountered are most directly comparable to those of which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 25–28 refer to the following quotation.

"MARY ELLIS DIED MAY 7th, 1845 … Such tokens were of common occurrence … we saw close before us the emigrant caravan, with its heavy white wagons creeping on in their slow procession, and a large drove of cattle following behind. … The women were divided between regrets for the homes they had left and apprehension of the deserts and savages before them." —Francis Parkman, The Oregon Trail: Sketches of Prairie and Rocky-Mountain Life, 1849 (abridged)
items.explanation: Like the Pilgrims, Parkman's emigrants were families enduring hunger, disease, and an unknown land to build new lives. Conquistadors sought plunder, astronauts were state-trained professionals, and cowboys were wage workers.

items.stem: Which of the following most directly anticipated and desired the movement Parkman described?
items.stimulus:
Questions 25–28 refer to the following quotation.

"MARY ELLIS DIED MAY 7th, 1845 … Such tokens were of common occurrence … we saw close before us the emigrant caravan, with its heavy white wagons creeping on in their slow procession, and a large drove of cattle following behind. … The women were divided between regrets for the homes they had left and apprehension of the deserts and savages before them." —Francis Parkman, The Oregon Trail: Sketches of Prairie and Rocky-Mountain Life, 1849 (abridged)
items.explanation: Jefferson envisioned a republic of independent farmers, which required vast new lands; his Louisiana Purchase made the overland migration possible. Hamilton preferred commerce and manufacturing; Franklin and Madison did not champion agrarian expansion the same way.

items.stem: Which of the following opinions from the 1960s most directly reflects McGovern's perspective?
items.stimulus:
Questions 29–32 refer to the following quotation.

In an April 25, 1967 speech, Senator George McGovern argued that the war had begun as a struggle among Vietnamese groups before American intervention, and charged that the United States seemed determined to save Vietnam from Ho Chi Minh even at the cost of destroying the country. —Paraphrase of George McGovern, "The Lessons of Vietnam," April 25, 1967 (abridged)

options.text: America must maximize its technological edge in Vietnam.
American bombing is producing step-by-step progress in Vietnam.
The American bombing campaign in Vietnam is a failure.
America must not give in to defeatism about Vietnam.

items.explanation: McGovern calls the intervention a self-defeating destruction of Vietnam, the core of the antiwar argument that bombing could not win the war. The other options all endorse the war effort.

items.stem: Sentiments like McGovern's most directly influenced which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 29–32 refer to the following quotation.

In an April 25, 1967 speech, Senator George McGovern argued that the war had begun as a struggle among Vietnamese groups before American intervention, and charged that the United States seemed determined to save Vietnam from Ho Chi Minh even at the cost of destroying the country. —Paraphrase of George McGovern, "The Lessons of Vietnam," April 25, 1967 (abridged)

options.text: Passage of the War Powers Act of 1973
The resignation of Richard Nixon in 1974
The emergence of a youth counterculture

items.explanation: Antiwar anger at an undeclared, open-ended war drove Congress to pass the War Powers Act over Nixon's veto, limiting presidents' ability to wage war without Congress. The Tet Offensive and Nixon's resignation had different causes.

items.stem: McGovern's sentiments most directly reflected which of the following popular attitudes that became widespread in the 1960s?
items.stimulus:
Questions 29–32 refer to the following quotation.

In an April 25, 1967 speech, Senator George McGovern argued that the war had begun as a struggle among Vietnamese groups before American intervention, and charged that the United States seemed determined to save Vietnam from Ho Chi Minh even at the cost of destroying the country. —Paraphrase of George McGovern, "The Lessons of Vietnam," April 25, 1967 (abridged)

options.text: The United States should embrace isolationism.
The United States should use force to spread American ideals abroad.
American commanders were not being given enough weapons in Vietnam.
Government statements about Vietnam could not be trusted.

items.explanation: By 1967 the 'credibility gap' had made distrust of official war claims a defining popular attitude. McGovern speaks for citizens who no longer believed what the government said about the war. Isolationism was never the antiwar position; the other options defend the war.

items.stem: Political discord during the Vietnam War most closely resembled the political divisions during which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 29–32 refer to the following quotation.

In an April 25, 1967 speech, Senator George McGovern argued that the war had begun as a struggle among Vietnamese groups before American intervention, and charged that the United States seemed determined to save Vietnam from Ho Chi Minh even at the cost of destroying the country. —Paraphrase of George McGovern, "The Lessons of Vietnam," April 25, 1967 (abridged)
items.explanation: The Mexican War also split the country, with critics like Lincoln and the Whigs calling it an unjust war of aggression. The Spanish-American War, World War I, and World War II each drew far broader initial support.

items.stem: The ideas expressed in Wheatley's poem most directly reveal the influence of which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following quotation.

"Some view our sable race with scornful eye, / 'Their colour is a diabolic die.' / Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain, / May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train." —Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773 (abridged)

options.text: The natural rights theory of John Locke

items.explanation: Wheatley's insistence that Black people share in Christian salvation and spiritual equality echoes the Awakening's message that all souls could be saved. She is arguing against racial hierarchy, not from Locke or from scientific racism.

items.stem: Wheatley's poem most directly reflects which of the following continuities in U.S. history?
items.stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following quotation.

"Some view our sable race with scornful eye, / 'Their colour is a diabolic die.' / Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain, / May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train." —Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773 (abridged)
items.explanation: Her poem is an early entry in the long American argument over whether Black people are entitled to equal moral standing, the same social-justice debate running from slavery through civil rights. It is not about church-state relations, immigration, or speech rights.

items.stem: The literary success of Phillis Wheatley led most directly to questions about which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following quotation.

"Some view our sable race with scornful eye, / 'Their colour is a diabolic die.' / Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain, / May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train." —Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773 (abridged)

options.text: The granting of political rights to women
The harsh treatment of pro-British Loyalists
The legitimacy of established churches in the states

items.explanation: An enslaved African woman publishing acclaimed poetry contradicted the racist claim that Africans were intellectually inferior, directly undermining slavery's justifications. It raised no comparable questions about women, Loyalists, or churches.

items.stem: The point of Wheatley's poem is best compared to which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following quotation.

"Some view our sable race with scornful eye, / 'Their colour is a diabolic die.' / Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain, / May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train." —Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773 (abridged)

options.text: Jonathan Edwards's sermon 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God'
The Seneca Falls Declaration of Rights and Sentiments
Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech

items.explanation: Both Wheatley and King argue from Christian morality for the essential equality of Black and white people. Edwards preached damnation, the Declaration announced political independence, and Seneca Falls addressed women's rights.

items.stem: In the Cooper Union Address, Lincoln called for which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following quotation.

"Wrong as we think slavery is, we can yet afford to leave it alone where it is … but can we, while our votes will prevent it, allow it to spread into the National Territories, and to overrun us here in these Free States? … LET US HAVE FAITH THAT RIGHT MAKES MIGHT, AND IN THAT FAITH, LET US, TO THE END, DARE TO DO OUR DUTY AS WE UNDERSTAND IT." —Abraham Lincoln, Cooper Union Address, February 27, 1860 (abridged)

options.text: Northern voters to resist pro-slavery demands
The seceded Southern states to return to the Union
More support for the war effort

items.explanation: Lincoln urges Northerners to stand by their duty and refuse to let slavery expand into the territories. No states had seceded yet in February 1860, there was no war to support, and he rejects middle-ground compromise as 'vain.'

items.stem: A member of which of the following political parties would most likely have supported Lincoln's position?
items.stimulus:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following quotation.

"Wrong as we think slavery is, we can yet afford to leave it alone where it is … but can we, while our votes will prevent it, allow it to spread into the National Territories, and to overrun us here in these Free States? … LET US HAVE FAITH THAT RIGHT MAKES MIGHT, AND IN THAT FAITH, LET US, TO THE END, DARE TO DO OUR DUTY AS WE UNDERSTAND IT." —Abraham Lincoln, Cooper Union Address, February 27, 1860 (abridged)
items.explanation: The Republican Party was founded in 1854 specifically to oppose slavery's expansion into the territories. Democrats were split but largely pro-slavery; the Federalists were long gone and the Progressives came decades later.

items.stem: In 1860, Lincoln and his supporters called for which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following quotation.

"Wrong as we think slavery is, we can yet afford to leave it alone where it is … but can we, while our votes will prevent it, allow it to spread into the National Territories, and to overrun us here in these Free States? … LET US HAVE FAITH THAT RIGHT MAKES MIGHT, AND IN THAT FAITH, LET US, TO THE END, DARE TO DO OUR DUTY AS WE UNDERSTAND IT." —Abraham Lincoln, Cooper Union Address, February 27, 1860 (abridged)

options.text: Blocking slavery's expansion into the territories
Strict enforcement of the Fugitive Slave Act

items.explanation: The Republican platform of 1860 demanded that slavery be kept out of the territories while tolerating it where it existed. Immediate abolition, war, and the Fugitive Slave Act were positions Lincoln explicitly did not take in 1860.

items.stem: Lincoln's Cooper Union Address is best compared to which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following quotation.

"Wrong as we think slavery is, we can yet afford to leave it alone where it is … but can we, while our votes will prevent it, allow it to spread into the National Territories, and to overrun us here in these Free States? … LET US HAVE FAITH THAT RIGHT MAKES MIGHT, AND IN THAT FAITH, LET US, TO THE END, DARE TO DO OUR DUTY AS WE UNDERSTAND IT." —Abraham Lincoln, Cooper Union Address, February 27, 1860 (abridged)

options.text: William Jennings Bryan's 'Cross of Gold' speech

items.explanation: Both the Cooper Union Address and the 'Cross of Gold' speech were electrifying convention-season orations that made their speakers the presidential front-runners of rising parties. The other choices are founding documents or wartime addresses.

items.stem: In 'The March of the Flag,' Beveridge supported which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following quotation.

"If England can govern foreign lands, so can America. If Germany can govern foreign lands, so can America. … Will you remember that we do but what our fathers did—we but pitch the tents of liberty farther westward, farther southward—we only continue the march of the flag?" —Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898 (abridged)

options.text: The Populist movement's program of economic reform
A new war against Great Britain
A sweeping reform of the Constitution
The creation of an American overseas empire

items.explanation: Beveridge argues that America can and should govern foreign lands, extending 'the march of the flag' beyond the continent. That is the imperialist case for keeping the Philippines and other 1898 acquisitions.

items.stem: Beveridge's speech was a response to which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following quotation.

"If England can govern foreign lands, so can America. If Germany can govern foreign lands, so can America. … Will you remember that we do but what our fathers did—we but pitch the tents of liberty farther westward, farther southward—we only continue the march of the flag?" —Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898 (abridged)
items.explanation: Delivered in September 1898, weeks after the Spanish-American War ended, the speech argues for annexing the war's spoils, especially the Philippines. Alaska (1867) and the Mexican War (1846–48) were long past.

items.stem: The theme of Beveridge's speech is most directly comparable to which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following quotation.

"If England can govern foreign lands, so can America. If Germany can govern foreign lands, so can America. … Will you remember that we do but what our fathers did—we but pitch the tents of liberty farther westward, farther southward—we only continue the march of the flag?" —Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898 (abridged)
items.explanation: Beveridge explicitly frames overseas expansion as continuing the continental 'march of the flag,' the Manifest Destiny argument of the 1840s carried across the Pacific. The Monroe Doctrine warned Europe off the hemisphere; containment and states' rights are unrelated.

items.explanation: Annexing an overseas empire made the United States a world power, the starting point of twentieth-century American global leadership. Imperialism is the opposite of isolationism, and the speech is about foreign policy, not economics or constitutional theory.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the colony of Pennsylvania?

William Penn's Charter of Privileges, granted to the inhabitants of Pennsylvania and the Territories on October 28, 1701, which guaranteed religious toleration and representative government.

options.text: A charter colony, in which the king granted a charter to colonists
A proprietary colony governed by a proprietor
A royal colony, in which the king appointed the governor
An independent colony operating outside the king's authority

items.explanation: Charles II granted Pennsylvania to William Penn personally, making it a proprietary colony: Penn and his heirs owned and governed it. It was neither a corporate charter colony, a royal colony, nor independent of the crown.

items.stem: William Penn was a member of which of the following persecuted religious groups?
items.stimulus:

William Penn's Charter of Privileges, granted to the inhabitants of Pennsylvania and the Territories on October 28, 1701, which guaranteed religious toleration and representative government.
items.explanation: Penn was a Quaker, and Pennsylvania was founded as a refuge for Quakers and other dissenters persecuted in England. Catholics founded Maryland; Puritans founded New England.

items.stem: Because of Penn's Charter of Privileges, Pennsylvania became known for which of the following?

William Penn's Charter of Privileges, granted to the inhabitants of Pennsylvania and the Territories on October 28, 1701, which guaranteed religious toleration and representative government.
items.explanation: The Charter's guarantee of religious toleration drew Quakers, Germans, Scots-Irish, and others, making Pennsylvania the most religiously diverse colony. Witch trials belong to Massachusetts; Penn welcomed faith, not suppressed it.

items.stem: In her speech, Eleanor Roosevelt alluded to an earlier threat to civil liberties created by which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 53–55 refer to the following quotation.

In a March 14, 1940 address to the American Civil Liberties Union, Eleanor Roosevelt said that traveling the country had made her conscious of the importance of civil liberties, warned that democracy is endangered whenever the light of liberty grows dim, and argued that while wartime nations lose freedoms of press, speech, and assembly, Americans at peace had a grave responsibility to guard them. —Paraphrase of Eleanor Roosevelt, address to the ACLU, Chicago, March 14, 1940 (abridged)
items.explanation: Roosevelt's warning recalls World War I, when the Espionage and Sedition Acts criminalized dissent. The New Deal and the Depression did not produce comparable speech prosecutions, and the Cold War came later.

options.text: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944 (the GI Bill)

items.explanation: Two years after her speech, Executive Order 9066 authorized the wartime internment of Japanese Americans, exactly the kind of liberty lost in wartime she had warned about. Social Security, the GI Bill, and the baby boom expanded opportunity rather than restricting liberty.
